name: Silymarin (milk thistle)

lead: Silymarin is the active extract of milk thistle, mainly sold as a liver-support supplement. People who take it for looks hope its antioxidant activity gives clearer, healthier-looking skin and slower visible ageing.

It is described as scavenging free radicals and chelating metals, with anti-inflammatory effects, and proposed skin benefits include protection from UV damage and inflammation. No human trials for skin or cosmetic outcomes were found.

paras: It is taken as a standardised capsule or tablet supplement, usually daily and over a long period. People pair it with ordinary skincare and sun protection rather than using it alone.
It may inhibit drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, so interactions with medicines cannot be excluded; pregnancy data are limited.

angle.text: Silymarin is a milk thistle liver supplement that some people take for its antioxidant chemistry, hoping for clearer skin or slower visible ageing. The skin role is proposed; no human skin trials were found.

lead: Silymarin is a standardised extract of the seeds of milk thistle (Silybum marianum), a Mediterranean-native plant. The extract is a complex of flavonolignans, chiefly silibinin (silybin), together with silychristin, silidianin and isosilybin, plus the flavonoid taxifolin.[1][2] It is sold mainly as a liver-support supplement and is one of the most widely studied herbal products for liver conditions.[3][4]

In looks-related communities its appeal is indirect and runs through two chains. One is skin: proposed antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and UV-protective actions that proponents hope will translate into calmer, clearer or better-protected skin.[1][5] The other is the 'liver support' habit common among people who use anabolic or other hepatically stressful compounds to build a physique, who list milk thistle alongside other liver-oriented supplements in training logs.[6][7] In both cases the supplement is a supporting habit rather than a direct appearance treatment.

Research on silymarin is concentrated on liver disease, with reviews and trials in fatty liver, cirrhosis, hepatitis and mushroom poisoning.[3][4][8][9] Wikipedia's article on silibinin notes proposed skin benefits such as protection against UV-induced damage and inflammation, drawn from laboratory work, and reports no human trials for skin or cosmetic use.[1]
infobox: Silibinin (silybin), a roughly 1:1 mix of silybin A and B[1]
Oral supplement; IV silibinin in Europe for Amanita poisoning[1]
Dietary supplement in many countries; oral hepatoprotective use approved in some EU states[1][2]

paras: Milk thistle is an annual or biennial thistle with white-veined leaves, native around the Mediterranean and naturalised in many temperate regions. Its fruit contains roughly 4-6% silymarin, and standardised commercial extracts concentrate this to about 65-80%.[2] Silymarin is a mixture of seven flavonolignans (silybin A and B, isosilybin A and B, silychristin, isosilychristin, silydianin) and the flavonoid taxifolin; silibinin is a semi-purified fraction that is roughly a 1:1 mix of silybin A and silybin B.[1][2]

Silymarin dissolves poorly in water and is poorly absorbed orally, which has driven formulations designed to raise bioavailability. These include a silymarin-phosphatidylcholine complex (silipide), cyclodextrin complexes and glycosylated silybin; a 2005 review cited by Wikipedia put the phospholipid complex at about ten times the bioavailability of plain silymarin.[1] A proprietary formulation, Eurosil 85, was developed to improve oral bioavailability, and much of the clinical liver research has used it.[3]

Intravenous silibinin (the water-soluble dihemisuccinate form, marketed in Europe as Legalon) is approved in Europe for poisoning by Amanita mushrooms; in the United States it is available only through expanded-access mechanisms.[1] Some European countries approve oral silymarin as adjunct therapy in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, and the European Medicines Agency's 2018 assessment report lists the hepatoprotective use as well established in 11 countries and traditional use for dyspepsia in four.[2] Elsewhere it is sold as a dietary supplement.[1]

Skin-related interest rests on laboratory findings that Wikipedia summarises: protection against environmental toxins, anti-inflammatory effects, reduced UVB-induced epidermal thickening, enhanced repair of UV-induced DNA damage and protection against UV-induced photocarcinogenesis and sunburn in experimental models.[1] These are presented as potential mechanisms, and the article cites no topical or oral trial of silymarin for skin appearance.[1]

In physique-focused circles, milk thistle is discussed less for skin than as part of a supplement stack. Forum members on T Nation list it among liver-oriented products taken during hard training, alongside fish oil, TUDCA, curcumin and similar items, including by people running anabolic-androgenic steroid cycles.[6][7][10] These posts are personal supplement lists, not research.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials in 2,375 people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease found that silymarin was associated with lower total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL cholesterol and fasting insulin, among other changes.[11] A randomised, double-blind trial in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis examined silymarin against placebo, and a 2024 randomised placebo-controlled trial in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease reported reduced liver stiffness linked with gut microbiota features.[12][13]

For chronic liver disease overall, reviewers describe the picture as encouraging in preclinical work but in need of larger, better-designed randomised trials; a pooled analysis of cirrhosis trials discussed in a 2020 narrative review and a separate meta-analysis summarised on Wikipedia found no effect on all-cause mortality.[1][4][8] A 1989 randomised trial in cirrhosis is among the older landmark studies.[14] The NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, as of 2020, reported no clinical evidence of a medicinal effect, according to Wikipedia's plant article.[2]

The best-described mechanism is antioxidant: silymarin is reported to scavenge free radicals directly, chelate iron and copper, and modulate enzymes involved in cellular damage, with downstream anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects described in liver models.[5][4][9] Further proposed actions include immunomodulation and, in cancer research, inhibition of STAT3 signalling.[1] Like other flavonoids, silymarin inhibits P-glycoprotein-mediated efflux and may inhibit some cytochrome P450 enzymes.[1]

Silymarin is generally described as well tolerated, with occasional stomach upset or allergic reactions; a 2019 safety review covers its toxicology.[15][2] Because it may affect drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, interactions cannot be excluded, although a 2017 review in American Family Physician places milk thistle among supplements with a low likelihood of clinically important interactions with most medications.[1][16] A 2022 review lists milk thistle among supplements associated with bleeding risk in patients on anticoagulants.[17]

In vitro work found that silibinin and silychristin block the MCT8 thyroid hormone transporter, though Wikipedia notes no published clinical evidence of thyroid problems.[1] Pregnancy data are limited.[1] Product quality is a reported concern: labelled silymarin content can differ from actual content, and a 2015 study found milk thistle supplements had the highest mycotoxin levels among tested plant supplements.[2] A phase I trial cited by Wikipedia in prostate cancer patients found very high daily doses well tolerated, with asymptomatic liver enzyme and bilirubin rises the most common adverse event.[1]

Milk thistle has a long record in European herbal medicine. Ancient Greek writers including Dioscorides described thistle-like plants, and the white leaf veins gave rise to the folk name 'Mary thistle', linked in legend to the Virgin Mary's milk.[18] The seed was used for centuries for liver and gallbladder complaints, which is the lineage modern silymarin products draw on.[9][2] Standardised extracts and the isolation of silibinin as the main constituent came with 20th-century pharmaceutical development in Europe.[1][4]

Silymarin is a common ingredient in liver-support and detox supplements and appears in beauty-from-within and skin supplement lines. In forum discussion it is typically listed as one item among many; one T Nation poster relayed that a physician told them milk thistle was the only supplement with even minimal liver benefit, a personal anecdote rather than research.[19] Regulators outside Europe generally classify oral milk thistle as a dietary supplement rather than a medicine.[1]

No studies found of silymarin for appearance or skin-cosmetic outcomes. Clinical research concerns other conditions: liver disease including NAFLD, NASH and cirrhosis,[4][8][11][12][13][14] chemotherapy-related liver injury in children,[20] and behavioural conditions. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with gambling disorder has been published,[21] and registered trials include trichotillomania (NCT02473913, 22 participants) and body dysmorphic disorder (NCT02843451, withdrawn before enrolment).[22][23]

Other registered studies cover pharmacokinetics and bioavailability in 16 healthy volunteers (NCT06882681), drug-interaction work with the HIV drug indinavir (NCT00011635), and fatty liver in 120 people with type 2 diabetes (NCT07871370).[24][25][26]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, milk thistle appears mostly in supplement lists, often as a 'liver support' item for people on anabolic regimens or heavy training, with occasional questions about substituting it for other products.[6][7][10]

timeline.event: Dioscorides describes thistle-like plants used in Greek medicine, an early part of the plant's recorded use.[18]
Linnaeus describes the plant as Carduus marianus; it is moved to the genus Silybum in 1791.[18]
A randomised trial of silymarin in cirrhosis is published in the Journal of Hepatology.[14]
The European Medicines Agency publishes an assessment report on oral milk thistle fruit, listing well-established hepatoprotective use in 11 countries.[2]
A meta-analysis of 26 trials in fatty liver disease is published.[11]
